title: The Afternoon Brief: Conferences move first; courts decide next
dek: The Big Ten and SEC banned players with pro experience from college competition, directly confronting a Louisiana court order allowing their return. Elsewhere, the NFL closed out the Seahawks sale at a record $9.612 billion, the WNBA hit 3.31 million viewers, and MLB proposed its most aggressive CBA restructuring yet, compressing free agency to three weeks.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Legal authority over player eligibility is now in direct conflict: conference rules prohibit what courts have already permitted, setting up a test of institutional versus judicial power before the August 31 hearing in Louisiana.
bottom_line: The Big Ten and SEC's ban on players with pro experience collides directly with a Louisiana court order allowing their return, and the August 31 hearing will test whether institutional or judicial authority governs college eligibility. Elsewhere, the WNBA hit a 29-year viewership record, MLB proposed its most aggressive labor restructuring yet with a December free-agency window, and the NFL closed the Seahawks' record $9.612 billion sale. The coming days will test whether courts enforce their rulings against conference policy, whether the county approves the Rays stadium deal Friday, and whether MLB's salary-cap demand dooms the broader free-agency restructuring as December 1 approaches.
body: The day's defining tension is not new but now sharpened: who controls whether a player can return to college after entering the professional process. On Tuesday, the Big Ten voted unanimously to ban football players who have signed pro contracts, appeared on pro rosters, or declared for the NFL Draft as underclassmen from competing in college. The SEC announced identical football rules the same night and extended the prohibition to basketball players with NBA and WNBA experience. Both conferences acted in direct response to a Louisiana state court's temporary restraining order issued last week, which allowed a group of players who participated in NFL training camp and preseason to return to college. The court ruled they would not have entered the professional process had they known college eligibility would remain available. That order extends until a hearing on August 31. The bans create a direct collision: conference rules now prohibit exactly what a state court has already ordered allowed. How LSU proceeds with the players named in the restraining order will reveal whether courts or conferences retain authority. The NCAA, which called such rulings "destabilizing," faces its own authority questions as it navigates conflicting judicial and institutional mandates.

Outside the courtroom, three other institutional shifts moved forward. NFL team owners voted unanimously Wednesday to ratify the league-record $9.612 billion sale of the Seattle Seahawks to a group led by venture capitalist Vinod Khosla's family, ending nearly three decades of Paul Allen family ownership and representing a 59 percent increase over the previous NFL record, the $6.05 billion Commanders purchase in 2023. The deal is expected to close in September. One constraint remains: the Khosla family holds a minority stake in the San Francisco 49ers and must divest that interest under NFL ownership rules.

In media and rights deals, two sports moved to reshape their broadcast posture. The NFL ended its nearly 80-year Pro Bowl competition, replacing the televised all-star game with a recognition-only honor bestowed on 88 selected players. The move follows three years of declining viewership, dropping from 6.7 million in 2023 to 1.9 million in 2026. The WNBA, meanwhile, secured a new partner after Victory+ collapsed: Roku will stream the league's Sunday night package free on the Roku Sports Channel beginning August 30, covering eight remaining regular-season games and continuing into 2027 with 25 games. The shift expands the Sunday night reach to a platform with substantially larger distribution as the WNBA heads into a competitive media rights market in 2027 when all national deals renew.

Caitlin Clark's Fever and the Chicago Sky drew 3.31 million viewers on NBC and Peacock, the most-watched WNBA regular-season game since the league's opening weekend in 1997. The Indiana Fever won 113-90, with Clark finishing with 37 points and 10 assists and Kelsey Mitchell adding 30 points. Late in the third quarter, former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Wintrust Arena after a verbal altercation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud. Sky owner Michael Alter stated that security rightfully removed Freedom after he became a threat by stepping forward; one courtside fan contradicted that account, saying Freedom did not initiate the altercation. The Chicago Sky placed an indefinite ban on Freedom attending Sky home games, though league sources told the desk that Freedom is not banned from other WNBA games as a fan. The exact nature of what sparked the confrontation remains contested.

On the labor front, MLB formally sent the players union a proposal Thursday that would restrict free-agency signings to a narrow December window followed by a complete ban on all player transactions through early February. The proposal opens at the first day of the winter meetings in December and closes December 21, creating what the league calls concentrated offseason urgency similar to the NFL and NBA. It also includes a quieter period for re-signings, reduced injured-list minimums, and expanded Rule 5 Draft eligibility. All proposals, MLB stated, require a salary cap and salary floor system. The players union rejected the proposal the same day. Bruce Meyer, interim executive director of the MLBPA, said MLB conditioned the proposals on the union accepting a salary cap that "would drastically reduce overall player compensation, eliminate fully guaranteed contracts through escrow, and turn back the clock on fundamental player rights." He called the free-agency window "an artificial window, subject to a salary cap, which would reduce player leverage and create a game of musical chairs pitting player vs. player." The union's immediate rejection signals that the salary-cap demand will dominate bargaining, not the free-agency window mechanics. The current CBA expires December 1.

Other moves: Liverpool agreed to a $120 million deal with Paris Saint-Germain for winger Bradley Barcola, comprising a guaranteed $100 million plus $20 million in add-ons tied to individual and team success, ending months of haggling over PSG's initial $145 million ask. Masai Russell of the United States ran 12.09 seconds in the women's 100m hurdles at the Diamond League meet in Zurich, and Alison Dos Santos of Brazil ran 45.80 seconds in the 400m hurdles, each breaking the world record in their discipline. The Ravens placed center Danny Pinter on injured reserve after he tore his patellar tendon during a joint practice with Minnesota, ending his 2026 season and forcing the Ravens to turn to Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic at the position. Unrivaled announced a Series C funding round securing more than $100 million and valuing the women's 3-on-3 basketball league at $650 million, nearly double the $340 million assessment from September 2025, with players retaining 30% ownership. Tampa City Council voted 4-3 Thursday to approve the city's participation in a $2.36 billion Rays ballpark project, advancing the decades-long stadium saga to a final county commission decision on Friday.
